title: workload-slice-bench-diary
content:
Summary:

This is a working diary capturing the design, experiments, and early regression triage for the workload-slice benchmarking harness. Goal: build a lightweight, reproducible microbench + trace-slicing pipeline that exercises kernel scheduling, KV cache behavior, and tail-latency under realistic request mix shifts. This is intentionally informal — notes, hypotheses, and action items are here so other engs can iterate quickly.

Why workload-slicing?
- Full trace replay is expensive and brittle for quick iterations.
- Pure microbench kernels (single-op latency) miss cross-cutting effects: scheduler backpressure, KV cache hit-rate interactions, and early-prefetch behavior.
- Slice traces into focused, parameterized workloads (prompt-length distribution, conversation-turn distributions, cache-affecting prefixes) that are small, repeatable, and tunable.

High-level approach:
1) Ingest production traces (anonymized token streams + metadata).
2) Define slice templates (e.g., short-single-turn, multi-turn-long-memory, streaming-chat-burst).
3) Generate workload artifacts: input batches, KV initial states, and time-offset arrival patterns.
4) Run microbench harness on target instance types (A100/H100), toggling kernel variants and scheduler knobs.
5) Collect epoch-level metrics/time-series and compare against baseline using statistical tests.

Experimental setup (current):
- Hardware: 1x H100-80GB (driver nodes used for kernel builds), 2x A100-80GB for cross-compare.
- Runtime commit: serving-runtime@f2c19b3 (branch: workload-slice-local).
- Kernel variants: flash_attn_v2, fused_mha_opt, unfused_reference.
- Quant modes: fp16, int8-ggml-like (profiling only).
- Scheduler variants: default-priority, latency-first, cost-aware-batching.
- KV cache modes: cold (empty), warm-fixed (50% hit), warm-dynamic (trace-derived).
- Target SLOs: p99 latency <= 280ms for short-single-turn workloads; steady-state throughput target 120 qps for medium batch sizes.

Slice templates (examples used so far):
- SHORT_SINGLE_TURN: 8–32 tokens prompt, 32–64 tokens gen, arrival poisson lambda tuned to keep util ~40–60% (baseline).
- MULTI_TURN_MEMORY: 6 turn conversation, earlier turns seed KV cache to create >70% hit-rate for later turns.
- STREAM_BURST: streaming tokens with small increments (1–8 tokens/chunk) to test continuous batching logic and early flush thresholds.
- LONG_PREFIX_HIT: very long prompt prefix (1024–2048 tokens) then short generation; stress KV eviction and KV-merge cost.

Metrics we capture (per-run, exported as CSV + JSON time-series):
- request latency distribution (p50,p90,p95,p99).
- per-token generation time (mean, std).
- kernel invocation counts and per-kernel latency.
- scheduler queue length over time and batch sizes selected.
- KV cache hit/miss counts, eviction churn, and memcopy time.
- GPU occupancy metrics (SM utilization), memcpy H2D/D2H durations.
- variance and skew tests across replay epochs.

Recent microbench runs (notes):
- SHORT_SINGLE_TURN, H100, fp16, flash_attn_v2:
  - p50: 45ms, p95: 120ms, p99: 260ms (baseline target close but p99 creeping above).
  - Observed that occasional 1–2s spikes correlated with kernel fallback to unfused_reference — caused by kernel-selector timeout when sequence-length unexpectedly rose above sampling bin.
  - Hypothesis: kernel selection uses stale percentile estimates from earlier epoch; need faster adaptive re-sampling or weight decay on long-tail bins.

- MULTI_TURN_MEMORY, A100, fused_mha_opt:
  - KV hit-rate configured ~75%; steady throughput 95 qps (below throughput target).
  - Bottleneck trace: host-side serialization between request packing and KV prefetch was blocking GPU submission; CPU-side batching microbenchmark shows syscall overhead at high small-batch rates.
  - Action: add per-core submission queue to reduce syscalls and explore splice-style zero-copy path.

Trace-based regressions discovered:
- Regression window: around runtime@b7e8cc5 we saw a 10% increase in p95 for streaming workloads.
- Root cause: changed prefetch policy that attempted speculative KV warming across requests; under heavy multi-tenant noise it produced bursts of memcpy H2D that preempted compute kernels.
- Short-term mitigation: revert speculative-prefetch flag in scheduler for streaming path.
- Long-term fix: bounded prefetch budget and prefetch priority low so it yields under compute pressure.

Anomaly hunting notes (examples):
- Symptom: sudden p99 tail appearing only at night (low-util periods).
  - Trace: aligned with weekly snapshot job that runs inside same cluster namespace causing network bursts.
  - Fix: better isolation and qos for snapshot job; tag snapshot requests so scheduler deprioritizes them for noisy host IO.

- Symptom: microbench shows kernel latency variance correlated to memcpy size distribution.
  - Investigation: memcpy fused with kernel launch in driver caused occasional driver polling that bumped latency.
  - Mitigation: move to asynchronous memcpy + event-driven batching to decouple copy from kernel launch.

Statistical comparison methodology:
- Each experiment runs 10 epochs (5 warmup, 5 steady-state). We compare steady-state epochs.
- Use paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test for median shifts and bootstrap CI for p99 changes (p99 is heavy-tailed, so nonparametric bootstrap preferred).
- Define regression as statistically significant shift (p < 0.05) and effect size > 8% for p95 or > 15% for p99.

Small reproducibility checklist (to attach to CI jobs):
- seed trace snapshot id and anonymization salt.
- kernel build id and git ref.
- docker image hash for harness.
- hardware SKU + driver versions.
- configuration flags (scheduler, kv mode, quant mode).

Open hypotheses and experiments to run next:
1) Adaptive kernel selector with exponential backoff on long-sequence bins: reduce oscillations that cause fallback. Plan: add per-sequence-length bloom counters and decay factor; run A/B vs current selector.
2) Per-core GPU submission queues + splice zero-copy: reduces syscall overhead observed in small-batch multi-turn workloads. Plan: microbench syscall cost and run on A100.
3) Bounded speculative prefetch budget: implement tokenized budget per shard; measure memcpy budget vs compute occupancy.
4) Streaming flush thresholds: experiment with dynamic flush (based on recent per-token latency) to keep p99 stable under bursty arrivals.

Action items (short-term):
- [Evan] revert speculative-prefetch flag on streaming path (PR linked). Target: hotfix to canary cluster. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1246)
- [Luis] prototype per-core submission queue and run syscall microbench.
- [Maya] add bootstrap CI job that runs workload-slice SHORT_SINGLE_TURN nightly and reports p95/p99 trends to datadog.
- [Priya] produce sanitized trace snapshot for public reproducibility and upload to confluence page.

Notes on harness implementation details (for engineers):
- Slices are stored as JSON artifacts that include: arrival timestamps (relative epoch), input-token arrays, kv-priming pairs (key->tensorref ids), and expected cache-hit vectors. Harness can optionally synthesize arrival curves (poisson/gamma/bursty).
- A lightweight runner (python + gRPC client) replays inputs and can inject controlled jitter. The runner records per-request timing using monotonic clock and an optional GPU timestamping extension (when driver allows).
- Microbench adapters: small C++ binary that can invoke single kernels repeatedly with pinned memory and collects full CUDA event traces. Use this for kernel-latency baselines outside the full runtime.

Logging and observability additions requested:
- Expose per-request kernel-selection decision in debug trace (kernel_name, time_decision, fallback_reason).
- Emit KV-cache eviction events tagged with shard id and score to correlate with p99 spikes.
- Add a low-overhead sampler that records 1/1000 requests full trace to S3 for offline forensic.

Appendix: quick results snapshot (most recent run: 2026-02-23)
- SHORT_SINGLE_TURN, H100, default-scheduler, flash_attn_v2: p50 42ms, p95 118ms, p99 275ms.
- SHORT_SINGLE_TURN, H100, latency-first scheduler: p50 44ms, p95 110ms, p99 210ms (latency-first reduced tail but reduced throughput by 12%).
- MULTI_TURN_MEMORY, A100, fused_mha_opt + per-core-submission-proto: throughput 118 qps (meets target), p95 190ms, p99 420ms (p99 still large due to eviction churn).

Concluding thoughts:
The workload-slice approach is proving useful: it narrows down surface area for root-cause while still exercising meaningful interactions between scheduler, kernel selection, and KV cache. Immediate focus: stabilize kernel-selection paths and reduce CPU-side serialization. Longer-term: fold the harness into CI as a smoke/regression gate for scheduler and KV changes.

If you want to reproduce any run, ping me (Evan) and I’ll hand off the snapshot id and docker hash.

Changelog:
- 2025-11-08: initial draft and first slice templates.
- 2025-12-15: added statistical methodology and short reproducibility checklist.
- 2026-01-19: recorded early regression and speculative-prefetch rollback plan.
- 2026-02-27: added per-core submission proto results and updated action items.
